explain.say: How does a whole country know how fast prices are rising? It goes shopping, sort of! Officials track the price of a giant pretend shopping basket. Look at the checklist: six steps to measuring inflation.

explain.say: See the first step: pick a basket, a list of hundreds of things families really buy, like rice, bus fares, phone bills and school shoes. It is weighted, which means things families spend more on count more. What would be in your family's basket?

explain.say: Now add up the cost. Say the whole basket cost 200 last year and costs 210 this year. Look at the blocks: 200 plus 10 makes 210. The rise is 10. Can you see the extra ten?

To get the rate, divide the rise by last year's cost: 10 divided by 200 is 0.05, which is 5 percent. That number comes from the CPI, the Consumer Price Index. Quick check: what if the rise was 20? Yes, 10 percent!

faq.q: What is in the shopping basket?
faq.a: Hundreds of goods and services that typical households buy: food, rent, fuel, transport, clothes, phone bills, school fees and more. Each country chooses its own list.
asks: What goods are in the CPI?

faq.q: How is the inflation rate worked out?
faq.a: Take this year's basket cost minus last year's, divide by last year's cost, and multiply by 100. From 200 to 210 is a rise of 10, and 10 divided by 200 is 5 percent.
The Consumer Price Index tracks the cost of the typical basket over time. The yearly change in the CPI is the most common measure of inflation.

faq.q: Why do they change the basket?
faq.a: Because what people buy changes. New things like smartphones are added, and things few people buy anymore are removed, so the basket stays realistic.

faq.q: Does everyone feel the same inflation?
faq.a: No. If food prices jump, poorer families, who spend more of their money on food, feel it more. Your own inflation depends on what you buy.
asks: Why does inflation feel worse for some people?

facts: In India, the Consumer Price Index is published monthly by the National Statistics Office.
Inflation rate = (new basket cost minus old cost) divided by old cost, times 100.

quiz.say: A basket cost 200 last year and 210 this year. What is the inflation rate?
quiz.show: A basket cost 200 last year and 210 this year. What is the inflation rate?
quiz.why: The rise is 10, and 10 divided by 200 is 5 percent.

wrong.0: 10 is the rise in money, not the percentage.
wrong.2: 210 is the new cost, not the rate of change.

quiz.say: Why is the basket updated from time to time?
quiz.show: Why is the basket updated from time to time?

options.show: People buy different things over time
options.say: People buy different things over time

quiz.why: Updating keeps the basket like what families really buy.

wrong.0: Changing the list does not change prices in shops.
